topic.subject: science
topic.title: Heart, blood vessels and double circulation
topic.scope: Four chambers, arteries vs veins (direction, not oxygen content), pulmonary circulation, pulse and heartbeat, blood pressure, heart attack vs cardiac arrest, blood is red in veins not blue, valves preventing backflow

nodes.name: Structure and working of the heart
Chambers and valves
Heart has four chambers: two upper atria, two lower ventricles
A septum separates the right and left sides
Valves let blood flow one way and stop backflow
Ventricle walls are thicker than atrial walls, left thickest
external_prereqs: muscle strength relates to work done

nodes.name: Heartbeat and pulse
Heartbeat is contraction then relaxation of heart muscle
Pulse felt at the wrist equals the heartbeat rate
Heart works involuntarily all life, resting briefly between beats
Blood vessels
Types of blood vessels
Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it towards the heart
external_prereqs: meaning of away from and towards

nodes.name: Capillaries are tiny thin-walled vessels where exchange happens
Arteries have thick elastic walls, veins thinner walls with valves
Blood colour and oxygen content
Oxygen-rich blood is bright red, oxygen-poor blood dark red
Blood in veins is never blue; veins look bluish through skin
external_prereqs: light absorption and scattering by skin

nodes.name: Pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood, pulmonary vein oxygen-rich blood
Double circulation and blood pressure
Pathway of blood
Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle to lungs to left atrium
Systemic circulation: left ventricle to body to right atrium
Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete round
Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood stay separate
Blood pressure and heart problems
external_prereqs: pressure as force on an area

nodes.name: Blood pressure is the force of blood on vessel walls; systolic over diastolic
external_prereqs: pressure as force on an area

nodes.name: Heart attack is blocked blood supply to heart muscle; cardiac arrest is the heart stopping
external_prereqs: heart muscle also needs blood supply

misconceptions.statement: The heart has two chambers, a left and a right.
misconceptions.why: Diagrams and the heart symbol show a left and right half, and students overlook the atria and ventricles.
misconceptions.fix: The human heart has four chambers: two atria on top and two ventricles below.

probe.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
probe.wrong_answer: Two

misconceptions.root_belief: what the simple picture shows is all there is

misconceptions.statement: The heart is on the left side of the chest and is shaped like a love symbol.
misconceptions.why: Everyday heart symbols and the feeling of the beat on the left shape this idea.
misconceptions.fix: The heart lies in the middle of the chest, tilted slightly left, and is a fist-sized muscular pump, not a love-symbol shape.

probe.question: Where is the heart located in the chest?
probe.wrong_answer: Completely on the left side, shaped like a love symbol

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's drawings and ideas about the body's internal organs

misconceptions.statement: Blood can flow directly from the right side of the heart to the left side through the middle.
misconceptions.why: Students picture the heart as one open bag with a wall that is only a line in diagrams.
misconceptions.fix: A thick wall called the septum separates the right and left sides, so blood must go through the lungs to reach the left side.

probe.question: How does blood from the right atrium reach the left atrium?
probe.wrong_answer: It passes straight through the middle of the heart

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student mental models of the circulatory system

misconceptions.statement: Valves are there to pump blood, not to stop it flowing backwards.
misconceptions.why: Students link everything in the heart to pumping and do not think of one-way gates.
misconceptions.fix: Valves act like one-way doors that open for forward flow and close to stop blood flowing back.

probe.question: What is the main job of heart valves?
probe.wrong_answer: To pump blood out of the heart

misconceptions.root_belief: every part of a system does the main job

misconceptions.statement: Only the heart has valves; veins have none.
misconceptions.why: Valves are taught with the heart and students do not carry the idea to the limbs.
misconceptions.fix: Large veins, especially in the legs and arms, also have valves that stop blood falling back as it returns to the heart.

probe.question: Which vessels have valves apart from the heart?
probe.wrong_answer: None, only the heart has valves

misconceptions.root_belief: a feature belongs to only one famous place

misconceptions.statement: All four chambers have equally thick walls.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams often draw chambers with similar outlines.
misconceptions.fix: Ventricles have thicker walls than atria, and the left ventricle is thickest because it pumps blood to the whole body.

probe.question: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not thicker; all walls are the same

misconceptions.root_belief: things that look alike work alike

misconceptions.statement: The heart beats only when it contracts; the 'lub' and 'dub' sounds are the heart opening and closing like a door.
misconceptions.why: Students think of the heart as a bag that only squeezes, and hear sounds as the muscle itself.
misconceptions.fix: A heartbeat is contraction followed by relaxation of the heart muscle, and the lub-dub sounds come from the valves closing.

probe.question: What causes the lub-dub sound of the heart?
probe.wrong_answer: The heart muscle opening and closing

misconceptions.root_belief: a process is only its most visible half

misconceptions.statement: Pulse is a separate rhythm made by the wrist vessel, not related to the heart.
misconceptions.why: The pulse is felt far from the chest, so students treat it as local.
misconceptions.fix: Each pulse is the wave of pressure from a heartbeat felt in an artery near the skin, so pulse rate equals heart rate.

probe.question: Why does the pulse rate at the wrist match the heart rate?
probe.wrong_answer: It does not; the wrist makes its own beat

misconceptions.root_belief: effects far away have separate causes

misconceptions.statement: Pulse can be felt in veins as well as arteries.
misconceptions.why: Students treat all blood vessels as the same and do not know pressure waves fade by the veins.
misconceptions.fix: The pulse is felt only in arteries, because the pressure wave from the heartbeat is lost before blood reaches the veins.

probe.question: A pulse is felt in which vessel: artery or vein?
probe.wrong_answer: Both arteries and veins

misconceptions.root_belief: a property of one type applies to all kinds

misconceptions.statement: The heart never rests, so it is never relaxed at any moment.
misconceptions.why: Teachers say the heart works non-stop, which students take literally.
misconceptions.fix: The heart muscle relaxes briefly after every contraction; these tiny rests add up over a lifetime.

probe.question: Does any part of the heart ever relax during a heartbeat?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is always contracting

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry oxygen-poor blood in every case.
misconceptions.why: The usual systemic example is taught first and then treated as a rule of vessel type.
misconceptions.fix: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood towards it; oxygen content depends on the circuit, so the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.

probe.question: Do all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one example works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on school students' understanding of the circulatory system

misconceptions.statement: The pulmonary vein carries oxygen-poor blood because it is a vein.
misconceptions.why: Students link veins with deoxygenated blood and ignore the direction of flow.
misconceptions.fix: The pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium; the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

probe.question: What type of blood does the pulmonary vein carry?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxygen-poor blood

misconceptions.root_belief: the name of a thing fixes what it carries
misconceptions.source_hint: concept inventories and misconception studies on circulation

misconceptions.statement: Blood leaves the vessels at tissues and flows freely around the cells.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine blood as a liquid that spills out to deliver things.
misconceptions.fix: Blood stays inside capillaries, and oxygen and nutrients pass through the thin capillary walls to the cells.

probe.question: How does oxygen reach the body cells from blood?
probe.wrong_answer: Blood flows out of the vessels and bathes the cells

misconceptions.root_belief: delivery means the whole carrier moves across

misconceptions.statement: Veins have thicker walls than arteries because there are more of them.
misconceptions.why: Students link more vessels or more blood with stronger vessel walls.
misconceptions.fix: Arteries have thicker, elastic walls because blood leaves the heart at high pressure; veins have thinner walls and valves.

probe.question: Which has thicker walls, an artery or a vein?
probe.wrong_answer: A vein

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen-poor blood is a different colour from red, such as blue or purple.
misconceptions.why: Diagrams colour veins blue and red to show the difference.
misconceptions.fix: All human blood is red; oxygen-rich blood is bright red and oxygen-poor blood is a darker red.

probe.question: What colour is oxygen-poor blood in the body?
probe.wrong_answer: Blue

misconceptions.root_belief: a diagram's colours show real colours
misconceptions.source_hint: documented in studies of school students' ideas about blood and circulation

misconceptions.statement: Veins look blue because the blood inside them is blue until it meets air.
misconceptions.why: Blue veins seen through the skin and blood turning red on bleeding seem to support it.
misconceptions.fix: Blood in veins is dark red; veins look bluish only because of how skin and light show them, and blood is red from the start.

probe.question: Why does blood look red when you bleed from a vein?
probe.wrong_answer: It turns red when it touches air

misconceptions.root_belief: seeing is believing about appearance
misconceptions.source_hint: widely documented common misconception in biology education literature

misconceptions.statement: Blood goes from the heart to the lungs and then straight to the body without returning to the heart.
misconceptions.why: Students picture two separate loops from the heart, not a path through the left atrium first.
misconceptions.fix: Blood from the lungs returns to the left atrium of the heart and only then goes out to the body.

probe.question: Where does blood go after leaving the lungs?
probe.wrong_answer: Directly to the body

misconceptions.root_belief: a journey has no stops on the way
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student mental models of the circulatory system (single, double and unspecified loops)

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen-poor blood from the body goes straight to the lungs without passing through the heart.
misconceptions.why: Students think the heart only pumps blood to the body and ignore the right side.
misconceptions.fix: Body blood enters the right atrium, goes to the right ventricle, and is pumped to the lungs.

probe.question: After blood returns from the body, where does it go next?
probe.wrong_answer: Straight to the lungs

misconceptions.root_belief: the heart is one pump with one outlet

misconceptions.statement: Double circulation means two different bloods are circulating, one in each lung.
misconceptions.why: The word 'double' suggests two of something, such as two lungs.
misconceptions.fix: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice in one round: once through the lungs and once through the body.

probe.question: What does 'double circulation' mean?
probe.wrong_answer: Blood flows through both lungs at once

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mix in the heart so the body gets a mixed blood.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine the heart as one bag where all blood is stirred and have seen mixing in amphibian hearts.
misconceptions.fix: In humans the right and left sides are separate, so oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood never mix.

probe.question: Does oxygen-rich blood mix with oxygen-poor blood in the human heart?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they mix in the heart

misconceptions.root_belief: what happens in some animals happens in all
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about the heart and circulation

misconceptions.statement: Blood pressure is the pressure of the heart muscle on the chest, not of blood.
misconceptions.why: Students link pressure with squeezing and the cuff on the arm.
misconceptions.fix: Blood pressure is the force that blood exerts on the walls of blood vessels, shown as systolic over diastolic.

probe.question: What does a blood pressure reading measure?
probe.wrong_answer: The squeezing force of the heart on the chest

misconceptions.root_belief: a measure belongs to the object you touch

misconceptions.statement: A single blood pressure number such as 120 is the pressure; the second number is just an error range.
misconceptions.why: Students read readings like marks or a range and ignore the two phases of a beat.
misconceptions.fix: The first number is the pressure during contraction (systolic) and the second during relaxation (diastolic).

probe.question: What do the numbers 120 and 80 in a blood pressure reading mean?
probe.wrong_answer: 120 is the pressure and 80 is the error

misconceptions.root_belief: two numbers mean a value and its error

misconceptions.statement: Heart attack and cardiac arrest are two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.why: News and everyday speech use the terms interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: A heart attack is blocked blood supply to part of the heart muscle; cardiac arrest is when the heart stops pumping, often due to an electrical problem.

probe.question: Is a heart attack the same as cardiac arrest?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they mean the same

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: health education research on public understanding of cardiac terms

misconceptions.statement: The heart does not need its own blood supply because blood passes through its chambers.
misconceptions.why: Students see blood inside the heart and assume the muscle takes oxygen from it.
misconceptions.fix: Heart muscle gets oxygen from its own coronary arteries; a blockage there causes a heart attack.

probe.question: How does the heart muscle itself get oxygen?
probe.wrong_answer: Directly from the blood in its chambers

misconceptions.root_belief: an organ that handles a substance has it free
